reasons: Etymology fine (μέλι = mel; γλυκύς = dulcis with Greek dissimilation). But 'sweeter than honey' is a generic comparison found in unrelated traditions, and these are the only native words for 'honey' and 'sweet' in both languages, so the co-occurrence is automatic. The Plato anchor only quotes Il. 18.109 (derivative; the context there is anger, not speech). Plautus has an endearment; Lucretius 1.947 has an epithet + noun, not the comparative, inside a honey-cup simile with Greek models. The Vedic version renews both words, so it shows only the motif.

All three roots are exact cognates: āma = ὠμός (*h₂eh₃mó-), kravís = κρέας, ad = ἔδω. The anchors check: AVŚ 8.6.48 has demons who eat raw human flesh, and Il. 22.347 has Achilles wishing to eat Hector raw. Both are cannibal savagery. What lifts this above ordinary 'eat raw meat' is the agent compound and the curse context: Ved. āmā́d- (RV 10.87.7d, with adantu) ~ Gk ὠμηστής (< ὠμός + *h₁ed-), used of carrion birds and dogs that tear the enemy's body (Il. 11.454, 22.67). I also found AVŚ 11.10.18, where raw-eating vultures (āmādaḥ, gṛdhrāḥ) are to tear (radantām) the corpse; it closely matches Il. 11.454, where ὠμησταί tear (ἐρύουσι). In AV, āma qualifies māṃsa, not kravis, so the NPs are not identical. Ordinary dietetic use exists (Hippocrates), so medium risk.

amṛ́ta- = ἄμβροτος (*n̥-mr̥-tó-) as an epithet of gods, against a *mer- word for men (mártya-, from *mórto-, vs βροτός *mr̥tó-; same root, different grade and suffix). The Vedic anchors carry both poles in one clause (AVP 1.78.1 devāṁ + amṛtān + martyaḥ; AVŚ 6.41.6 amartyā + martyāṁ; also RV 4.2.1, RV 10.91.11). The Greek anchor is weaker: Plato quotes Aeschylus, the god word θεός is not cognate, and only the mortal pole βροτοῖς appears. The Homeric support confirms the figure (Il. 24.460 θεὸς + ἄμβροτος; 24.464 ἀθάνατον + βροτούς; Od. 5.218). Calling men 'mortals' and gods 'immortals' with the *mer- root is a specific lexical choice, not a universal one. The god word is renewed in Greek.

Ved. √tak- ~ Slavic teči (*tekʷ-) is a sound etymology, but there is no shared phrase. The animals are not cognate (śyená- vs соколъ; mr̥gá- vs вълкъ), and in the Slovo the falcon goes with полетѣ, not with a *tekʷ- verb. Only the wolf takes потече. In Slavic, *tekʷ- is the everyday verb 'run/flow' (cf. растекашеся, of thought). Similes comparing speed to predators are universal. The Slovo is a late (12th c. at best, authenticity debated) Old Russian text. Coincidence.

Both equations are sound: εὐρύς = urú-, and πόντος = pánthā- (with the 'passage' > 'sea' drift). Vedic urú- + pánthā- is checked in 4 RV anchors. The Greek anchor (Aeschines quoting Hes. Op. 246-7) is a mismatch: εὐρὺν agrees with στρατὸν, and πόντῳ stands alone. The real Greek collocation εὐρέα/εὐρέι + πόντον/πόντῳ is solid in support (Il. 6.291, Hes. Op. 650 checked). But 'wide' is the stock epithet of expanses in both languages (εὐρύς with οὐρανός, χθών; urú- with antárikṣa-, loká-), so the pairing is close to expected. Defensible, not compelling.

ἴς = uīs is fine. ἄνεμος ~ anima share a root (*h₂enh₁-) but differ in stem and in meaning. In Lucr. 3.397 the phrase is 'force of the soul', not wind, so that anchor is misread for the claim. Lucr. 6.578 (animae ... uis = air/wind) fits, but uis + genitive is Lucretius' productive idiom (uis + uenti 11x; 6.592 has uis + uenti, while impetus + animai is at 6.591). Lucretius knew Homer, so he may be imitating. 'Force of the wind' is generic. Nothing beyond the root match.

The cognates are right: addhí = ἔσθι (*h₁éd-dʰi); píba = bibe (*pi-ph₃-e); edo, ἐσθίω, πίνω. But 'eat and drink' is a universal merism made of the two basic verbs, so co-occurrence is expected in any corpus. The contexts are not congruent. Vedic invites a god to an offering. The Greek and Latin anchors are dietary prescriptions (Hippocrates uses jussive ἐσθιέτω/πινέτω; Cato has esse ... bibat across a conditional clause, and ederis + bibes + que). The tighter matches are in support (Od. 10.460) and stay generic.

reasons: *dyéw- + *ph₂tér: Ved. dyaúḥ + pitā́ = Gk Ζεῦ + πάτερ = Lat. Iuppiter. An exact two-member cognate collocation in apposition, used of the sky god in prayer, and specific (the deified sky named as father). Exact vocative match in RV 6.51.5a (dyaùḥ + pítar). Note: neither anchor passage line contains the formula. It sits in the context lines (RV 1.191.6a, Il. 1.503), both checked.

pátnī = πότνια (*pótnih₂) is exact. But δῖα (*diw-yo-) is not the cognate of devī́ (*deywih₂), so the second element is only root-related. Vedic pátnī here means 'wife': AVP 19.1.17 = RV 1.22.11 'goddesses, wives (nṛ-patnīḥ)', while Greek πότνια is an honorific 'lady'. Od. 1.14 has νύμφη + πότνια and δῖα + θεάων in separate phrases. Hes. fr. 150.31 is fine. The best Vedic parallel (RV 4.5.13 devī́ḥ + pátnīḥ) is support only. A title 'lady' for goddesses is plausible as inherited, but the pair as claimed is loose.

Same figure as B075/B093. The cognates are right (μέλι = mel, γλυκύς = dulcis), and Il. 1.249 (Nestor's voice) and Il. 18.109 check. But 'sweeter than honey' is a generic comparison, attested also outside IE, and the words are the default ones for 'honey' and 'sweet', so co-occurrence is automatic. Vedic renews both terms, which shows only the motif. Plautus (an endearment) and Lucretius (a honey-cup simile; epithet, not comparative) may follow Greek models.

Both are exact cognates: sána- = ἕνος (*séno-), náva-/návya- = νέος (*néwo-). Vedic sánā + návā + ca is a real coordinated pair (RV 8.45.25b). Greek ἕνη + νέα binomial checks (Ar. Nub. 1134 and passim; Lysias). What helps is that ἕνος survives in Greek almost only in this binomial (0 Homeric hits), which looks like a fossil. Against: 'old and new' is a generic polar merism. The contexts are unrelated (Indra's deeds vs. the last day of the month). RV 1.174.8a is predicative ('old came as new'), not the binomial.

Duplicate of B085, and the same verdict. Exact cognate members (sána- = ἕνος, náva- = νέος). The Greek fossil (ἕνη + νέα; Plato Crat. 409b glosses νέον + ἕνον of moonlight, checked) speaks for an old binomial. But this is the generic old/new merism, the Vedic and Greek contexts do not correspond, and RV 1.174.8a is predicative. RV 8.45.25b is the real Vedic pair. The Lithuanian senas + naujas pair is not checked.

ὄνομα = nā́man- (*h₁nómn̥) and τίθημι = √dhā (*dʰeh₁-), with the name as direct object, in the middle voice in both. Checked: Demosthenes Macart. 74 (ὀνόματα/ὄνομα + ἐθέμην, naming sons; everyday prose usage), RV 1.103.4d (nā́ma + dadhé), plus Od. 19.403/406 and 18.5 (naming a newborn), RV 10.115.2a, RV 5.3.10a, and Latin nomen + indo (PlCapt 69). Choosing 'put' over 'give/call' recurs in at least three branches. The Hittite lāman dai- is recalled and not verified. The Vedic anchor differs a little in sense (Indra takes a name for fame), but naming with dhā is also attested. *dʰeh₁- is a very general verb, so medium generic risk.

Only the noun is cognate (ā́yus- ~ αἰών). The adjective is renewed in Greek (μήκιστος/μακρός, not a δολιχός cognate). The Greek anchors are Xenophon prose with a superlative and a partitive genitive ('the longest span of human life'), not the collocation. The cognate pair dīrghám + ā́yuḥ = darəgə̄m + āiiū is Indo-Iranian only (and Y 31.20 is a 'long life of darkness', a punishment). 'Long life' is a generic expression in every language, and 'long-lived' compounds are trivial formations.

Same formula as B082 and B109: Ved. dyaúḥ + pitā́ (AVŚ 9.10.23, 6.120.4) = Gk Ζεῦ + πάτερ = Lat. Iuppiter (*dyew-ph₂ter, univerbated). Exact vocative in RV 6.51.5a. Anchor problems: in the Homeric anchors (Il. 15.371, 15.373) the formula is only in context line 15.372 (checked). AVŚ 6.120.3 has bhūmir + mātā, while dyaur + pitā is in s4. Catul 66.29 is irrelevant, and its context line 66.30 (Iupiter) is a translation of Callimachus, so it is derivative and adds nothing. Cato's Iane + pater and 'Iupiter' (CatAgr 134.2) are the real Latin witness. The claim is true despite these weak anchors.

Ved. dyauṣ + pitā (AVP 1.12.5, AVŚ 2.28.7, long-life charms with pṛthivī + mātā) ~ Lat. Iupiter < *dyew + *ph₂ter, fused into a theonym with oblique Iou-. The Cato unit CatAgr 132.1 contains Ioui and the vocative Iupiter (dapalis) in a prescribed prayer at an offering. The Latin evidence is the fusion itself: an old apposition explains it, generic god + 'father' does not. Greek Ζεῦ + πάτερ (Il. 1.503) confirms. Context comparable (ritual address).

The etymologies hold: √rej- = ἐλελίζω 'shake' (*h₁leig-; Beekes connects them and notes Ved. rejata + kṣā́ḥ ~ ἐλελίχθων), and tvíṣ- ~ σείω (*tweis-, Beekes after EWAia). The anchors check: RV 4.17.2a (tviṣáḥ, rejata, dyaúḥ), Il. 8.199 (σείσατο, ἐλέλιξε, Ὄλυμπον), HH 28.9 (σείσασ', ἐλελίζετ', Ὄλυμπος). But the *tweys- members do different jobs: in Vedic a noun for the god's fury, in Greek a verb for the god shaking herself or her spear. The trembling subject is renewed (dyaúḥ vs Ὄλυμπος, a defensible renewal). The cosmos trembling at a god's birth or anger is a widespread theophany motif. A real lexical pairing, but not compelling.

Same collocation as B087: τίθημι + ὄνομα = √dhā + nā́man, both cognate and in the same relation (name as object of 'put'), both often middle. Checked: RV 6.44.8c (dádhānaḥ + nā́ma), Od. 19.406 (τίθεσθ' + ὄνομ'), Od. 19.403, Od. 18.5, RV 10.115.2a (nā́ma + dhāyi, the name given), RV 5.3.10a. The Vedic middle means 'assume a name' and the Greek 'give a name', but the passive and active Vedic uses match the Greek. The Hittite witness is fragmentary or recalled. The general sense of *dʰeh₁- makes some independent formation possible, so medium risk.

Third version of the honey claim (B075/B084). The Greek anchor (Plato Ep. 13) has γλυκέος agreeing with οἴνου and μέλιτος as a separate item in a shipping list, which is no collocation. The Latin anchors (PlAsina 614; Lucr. 1.938, 1.947) are 'sweet honey' or 'sweeter than honey', which is generic: these are the only words for 'honey' and 'sweet', and honey is the universal standard of sweetness. Lucretius' honey-rimmed cup has Greek models.

āp- ~ Latv. upe (*h₂ep-) and tak- ~ tecēt (*tekʷ-) are acceptable etymologies. But 'the water/river runs' is a near-universal collocation, and both words are the everyday terms in each language. The grain/fertility link is thin: Av. VS19.26c lists water and grain items, while the Latvian songs have rivers of rye and wine. These are two traditions more than two millennia apart, and the Latvian evidence is OCR quotations. The anchors check, but co-occurrence is expected.

The cognates are exact: vácas- = ἔπος = Av. vacah- (*wékʷos), and √takṣ = Av. taš- = τέκτων, τεκταίνομαι (*tetḱ-). The collocation 'fashion words (like a carpenter)' is checked in all three branches: RV 6.32.1d (vácāṃsi + takṣam), Od. 14.131 (ἔπος + παρατεκτήναιο), Pind. P. 3.113 (ἐπέων + τέκτονες), and the Avestan compound vacastašti- (N15.1a, VrS36.4l). It is a specific metaphor, not generic. Caveat: the Greek anchor (Philebus 55e) is a false match (τεχνῶν and the idiom with ἔπος + εἰπεῖν). The proof is in the support.

The swift-horse part is sound (āśú-/āśīyas- ~ ὠκύς; áśva- ~ ἵππος; see B097), but the anchors do not show it. Il. 23.273 has ἱππῆας + ἀγῶνι and no 'swift'. The AVP line has a comparative 'swifter than wind' addressed to a horse. The contest word is not a cognate pair: ājí- (i-stem, 'race') and ἀγών (n-stem, 'gathering, arena') are separate derivatives of *h₂eǵ-. The horse-race setting is comparable. This is a widening of B097 with loose evidence.

āśú- = ὠκύς = Av. āsu- (*h₁oHḱú-) and áśva- = ἵππος = aspa- (*h₁éḱwo-). Both members are cognate in an attributive collocation: RV 1.117.9b (āśúm + áśvam), Il. 10.474 (ὠκέες + ἵπποι, 35 Homeric lines), and the Avestan compound āsu.aspa-, plus āśú- used substantively as 'steed' (RV 2.31.2c, 2.34.3b, with áśvān in 3a). Anchor note: RV 2.31.2c has āśávaḥ without áśva. 'Swift horses' is semantically natural, but the three-branch fixity (formula, compound, substantivised epithet) argues for an inherited phrase.

Same Sky-Father formula (dyaur/dyauṣ + pitā ~ Ζεύς + πατήρ ~ Iuppiter). Exact cognates, specific. The Vedic anchors check (AVŚ 9.10.23, AVP 1.12.5, with pṛthivī + mātā). Greek: Διὶ + πατρί is in the context line (Od. 24.518, a prayer before a cast), not in the passage line 24.519, which I checked.

δώτωρ/δωτήρ = dātár- (*deh₃-tor-), with genitive plural ἑάων ~ vásūnām (*h₁wesu-), as a divine epithet 'giver of goods'. Checked: Od. 8.335 (δῶτορ + ἑάων, a vocative to Hermes), Od. 8.325 (θεοί + δωτῆρες + ἑάων), and RV 8.51.5a (dātā́ + vásūnām). Greek ἐύς is otherwise almost lost as a noun, which suggests a fossil. The AV anchors are weaker: AVŚ 12.1 has the compound vasu + dāḥ for Earth; AVP 19.1.5 has vasu + patiḥ, a renewal. The formula itself holds, with congruent context (gods as givers of wealth).

In the anchors only paśu ~ pecus is cognate. The 'man' word is renewed on both sides (puruṣa- and homo, not cognate). In AVŚ 16.8.1, vīrā and paśavo are separate items of a long list, not a pair. Lucretius' plague (6.1092, men + herds) follows Thucydides, and 'men and cattle' struck by disease is generic. The fully cognate figure (*wiHro- *peḱu-) is real but support-only here (Umbr. ueiro + pequo, checked in Buck; Av. pasu + vīra; Cato 141.3 pastores + pecuaque); see B110. The phrase is genuine (B110), but this claim's own anchors do not carry the cognate pair, hence weak.

τέρπω ~ tṛp- (*terp-) is fine, but ātmán- ~ ἦτορ is not an accepted etymology. Beekes derives ἦτορ from *h₁eh₁t-r 'heart, intestines' (ON æðr, OIr. inathar) and does not mention ātmán. The AVP line (indro + marutvāṃs + tṛpta + ātmā) is syntactically unclear and is about satisfying with waters. Il. 9.705 is satiety with food and wine. 'Sated in heart' with a perfect participle + accusative of respect is a Greek-internal idiom. There is only one secure element.

The etymologies are fine: superus ~ upara- (*(s)upero-), inferus ~ aδara- (*n̥dʰero-). But 'upper and lower' is a universal polar pair, and each language uses its inherited adjectives automatically. The contexts differ: Plautus puns on those upstairs/downstairs (gods above/below) in a cooking joke, while the Avestan line speaks of lower/upper creations. PlCapt 305 has superlatives (summo/infumum), a different figure. Vedic renews the pair. Coincidence of vocabulary.

θύρα = foris (*dʰwer-) is fine. κλῄω and claudo are separate derivatives of *kleh₂w- (one denominative, one d-present), so there is no inherited verb phrase. 'Shut/bar the door' is material-culture wording any language forms with its door and bar words. The anchors (Vesp. 198, 335; Lucr. 4.598; PlAsina 759) are ordinary comedy and physics contexts. Generic.

The figure (gods 'immortal' *n̥mr̥tó- vs men 'mortal' *mr̥tó-/*mórto-) is real; see B077. But these anchors are poor. The Greek ones (Eur. HF 1 βροτῶν; Hipp. 91 βροτοῖσιν) only contain 'mortals' and are not congruent with the Vedic contexts (a vessel sewn by the immortal gods; Agni knowing gods and mortals). The Greek god + ἄμβροτος collocation is support-only (Il. 24.460, Od. 24.445, checked). RV 1.70.6b (devā́nām + mártān) is a decent polar pair. The phrase is genuine (B077), but this claim's own anchors do not carry it, hence weak.

Sky-Father formula with both members cognate in three branches: AVŚ 3.23.6 and 9.10.23 (dyauḥ/dyaur + pitā, with pṛthivī + mātā), CatAgr 132.2 (Iupiter + dapalis and Ioui in a prescribed offering prayer, the univerbated *dyew-ph₂ter), and Gk Ζεῦ + πάτερ (Il. 1.503 support). Also Diespiter (PlCapt 909, checked). Ritual context in both. Exact and specific.

The theme (the slain as food for scavengers) is shared, and Greek and Vedic do have a congruent cognate pair: Il. 1.4-5 'make (τεῦχε) prey for dogs (κύνεσσιν) and birds (οἰωνοῖσι)' ~ AVŚ 11.2 (DCS s5-s6) 'do not make (kartam) our bodies for the dog (śune) ... the birds (vayāṃsi) must not find them'. Dog = *ḱwṓ; οἰωνός and vayas both from *h₂ewi-, though with different formations. But the anchors are mostly non-cognate. Beowulf has wolf + raven + eagle; Catullus 108 is a Hellenistic-style curse (vulture, raven, dogs, wolves) and possibly derivative; Antigone 29 only has birds and echoes Homer; AVŚ 11.9.20 has birds sated on enemies. The verbs are renewed everywhere. Corpses left to dogs and birds is a near-universal motif (also Semitic), so generic risk is high.

The cognates are right: ἐγρήγορα ~ jāgṛ- (*h₁ge-h₁gor-); ὕπνος/svap- (*swep-). But 'waking or sleeping' is a generic merism for 'at all times'. In the Greek anchor (Rep. 476c) the sleep member is the noun ἐν + ὕπνῳ, and elsewhere Greek uses εὕδω/καθεύδω. The contexts do not correspond: Vedic expiation formulas for sin (AVŚ 6.115, 6.45, 6.96; RV 10.164.3) vs. Plato's epistemology of dreaming. The Vedic phrase is itself a single repeated formula, so the Indic side is one witness.

Only the kin terms are cognate (pitā/πατήρ/pater; mātā/μήτηρ/mater). In the Greek and Latin anchors the sky and earth words are renewed (οὐρανός and ἥλιος, γῆ; aether, terra). Aristotle reports common usage, and Lucretius' Pater + aether / Matris + terrai follows Greek philosophical and Euripidean models, so it is likely derivative. 'Earth mother, sky father' is cross-culturally common. The cognate core (dyaúḥ + pitā́ ~ Ζεῦ + πάτερ) is not in these anchors. The Vedic anchors (AVŚ 9.10.23, 3.23.6, 12.1.12) check. Defensible as a parent-pair figure, not compelling as wording.
checked_loci: grc:Aristoteles et Corpus Aristotelicum De generatione animalium 1.2.716a s7

reasons: The best-anchored Sky-Father claim. Vedic dyauś/dyaur + pitā (AVP 5.21.1 with pṛthivī + mātā, against fever; AVŚ 9.10.23). The Greek passage lines carry Ζεῦ + πάτερ as prayer openings (Il. 19.121, 5.421, Od. 7.331, Pind. I. 6.42). The vocative matches exactly: RV 6.51.5a dyaùḥ + pítar, and AVŚ 6.4 dyauṣ + pitar (checked). Lat. Iuppiter/Diespiter fused. Exact cognates, congruent function (invocation), specific.

Both members are cognate across Indo-Iranian and Italic: paśú- = pasu- = Umbr. pequo = Lat. pecu (*péḱu), and vīrá- = vīra- = Umbr. ueiro (*wiHró-). The formula appears as a fixed pair in welfare prayers. Checked: Y9.4e (pasu + vīra, in Yima's age none died), VS10.18c (pasu + vīra), Y45.9d (pasūš + vīrə̄ṇg), AVP 19.56.26/30/32 (paśubhiś + ca + vīraiḥ, an oblation refrain), Umbrian ueiro + pequo ... salua + seritu (Buck), and Cato 141.3 pastores + pecuaque + salua + seruassis (man-word renewed). Same function in all of them, not a casual co-occurrence. Low risk.

The cognates are acceptable: ὄφις/ἔχις ~ áhi- (*h₁ógʷʰi-, with irregularities), and γῆρας ~ jūrṇá- (*ǵerh₂-). The anchors check: Aristotle HA 8.17 (ἐκδύνει/ἐκδύνουσι + γῆρας) and RV 9.86.44c (áhiḥ, jūrṇā́m, tvácam, sarpati). The shared point is naming the slough with the 'grow old' root. But Vedic has 'old skin' (an adjective on tvác-), while Greek nominalises 'old age'. The verbs differ (ἐκδύω vs áti + sr̥p-). The snake shedding its age as an image of rejuvenation is widespread beyond IE. Plausible, but natural to coin independently.
